lines.text: Here's something that should be simple.
You've got USDC on an exchange. You want it in a savings app on Arc.
So you send it… and the app has no idea it's yours.
Exchanges and wallets can only send to an address.
But apps keep money in smart contracts, and those only accept it through their own deposit function. That's how they know who to credit.
Sending is easy. Getting it into the right contract is the hard part.
Doorstep closes that gap.
It turns an ordinary USDC transfer into a proper deposit, credited to the right person.
Here's how.
First, the app sets the instructions: the contract, who gets credited, and where refunds go.
Those instructions produce an address. Change anything, and you get a different one.
The payer just sends their USDC there, from a wallet or straight from an exchange.
Then a delivery bot calls the contract's deposit function for them. If it can't, the money goes back to the refund wallet.
And it's live on Arc mainnet.
In the demo, you get your own savings address, with a QR code and the instructions behind it.
Send a few cents, and watch it arrive in your savings.
Every payment gets a receipt, and Doorstep's cut is zero.
Behind it: an SDK on npm, a hosted API with signed webhooks, and a bot that runs around the clock.
Arc is what makes this practical, because gas is paid in USDC.
The bot spends USDC to deliver, and it's repaid in USDC from the payment, with a cap.
No second token. No price oracle. No swaps.
Apart from that capped fee, money only goes two places: into the contract in the instructions, or back to the refund wallet.
Nobody can redirect a payment, and there's no admin key at all.
It isn't audited yet, so keep the amounts small.
And because it's just an address, any app can use it.
Savings. Escrow. Invoices. Payroll.
Even AI agents: our MCP server lets them create, check and deliver payments, but never send money anywhere else.
Your users' money is already out there.
Doorstep gives it a way in.
